title: The rise and rise of Gustav Mahler
gist: The Spectator's chief classical critic uses BBC Proms programming data to show how fast a canon can re-rate: only two Mahler symphonies were played in full at the Proms in the 67 years from 1895 to 1962 (nine performances total), against four of his nine completed symphonies plus Das Lied von der Erde and the Rückert-Lieder in the 2026 season alone. He argues this refutes the 'gatekeeper' theory of the canon — living-memory gatekeepers were adamant Mahler be excluded — and flags Lili Boulanger and Erich Korngold as candidates creeping in next.

insights.claim: Between 1895 and 1962 only two Mahler symphonies, the First and Fourth, were played in full at the BBC Proms — nine performances in 67 years, to frequently bemused reviews — whereas the 2026 season features four of his nine completed symphonies plus Das Lied von der Erde, the Rückert-Lieder and Britten's 1941 transcription of a movement from the Third.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: A hard, auditable series showing a cultural asset going from near-zero programming to dominant share within a single lifetime — the base case for how fast reputational repricing can happen.
insights.locator: Between 1895 and 1962, only two Mahler symphonies

insights.claim: Mahler is now programmed so comprehensively at the Proms that, in the author's words, old masters like Beethoven and Tchaikovsky can only dream of being represented so fully.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: The re-rating overshot past the incumbents rather than merely reaching parity — the pattern of a crowded consensus trade.
insights.locator: A typical 21st century Proms season, in other words.

insights.claim: The 2026 Proms season includes two performances in which the Aurora Orchestra plays Mahler's hour-long First Symphony from memory — a marker of how thoroughly internalised the repertoire has become.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: Performing an hour-long work from memory signals repertoire saturation, the point at which novelty value is exhausted.
insights.locator: the 2026 season features four of Mahler’s nine completed symphonies

insights.claim: The BBC Proms has for 131 years combined determinedly audience-friendly programming with a willingness to gamble on the new or newly fashionable, and its searchable performance database makes it a usable data bank for tracking taste in the English-speaking concert hall.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: Names a specific, public, long-run dataset for measuring cultural taste shifts — a methodology transferable to other consensus-tracking problems.
insights.locator: Jump forward: the 2026 BBC Proms season

insights.claim: As late as early 1974, when Glenn Gould reviewed the first volume of Henry-Louis de la Grange's Mahler biography under the title 'Data Bank on the Upward-Scuttling Mahler', the underlying assumption of the piece was that Mahler was not necessarily a composer who needed to be taken seriously.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: A dateable snapshot of elite opinion just before it flipped — the kind of artefact that lets you locate the turning point of a consensus after the fact.
insights.quote: Data Bank on the Upward-Scuttling Mahler
insights.locator: In 1973 the musicologist Henry-Louis de la Grange

insights.claim: Reference works of the period recorded the prior consensus explicitly: Penguin's classic 1949 paperback The Symphony called Mahler 'vulgar' and said he 'seldom knew where he was going', while a 1955 volume in the authoritative Master Musicians series bundled him with Bruckner as an Austrian curiosity, neither composer deemed to warrant a book to himself.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: Authoritative reference works codified a judgement now considered absurd — a caution against treating current expert consensus as settled.
insights.locator: The textbooks in my school music library

insights.claim: In the author's teens in the 1980s he knew professional musicians who still regarded Mahler as a fad, and when his father bought his treasured LP set of Mahler's Seventh he warned that it was 'modern music' — whereas undergraduate musicians he taught in the 2010s were bewildered to learn Mahler had ever been marginal.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: Generational amnesia about the prior consensus is what makes the current one feel timeless — the same mechanism that makes any regime seem permanent to those inside it.
insights.locator: Does that come as such a surprise?

insights.claim: Popular culture preserves the transition: Sondheim's Company (1970) has a 'Ladies Who Lunch' character name-drop Mahler as Manhattan insider knowledge, Willy Russell's Educating Rita (1980) has a pseudish housemate ask 'Wouldn't you just die without Mahler?' marking him as a student cult, and by 2000 neither joke worked because he had become a classic.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: Jokes stop landing when the referent moves from niche to mainstream — a dateable, low-cost indicator for when an asset has completed its transition to consensus.
insights.quote: Wouldn’t you just die without Mahler?
insights.locator: Popular culture, meanwhile, has preserved a few relics

insights.claim: The current popularity of huge areas of the baroque repertoire including Monteverdi, Vivaldi and many of Handel's operas dates substantially from the late-1970s explosion in historically informed performance and the 1980s compact disc boom, with Vivaldi's Four Seasons first heard at the Proms only in 1984.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: A technology shift (the CD) plus a performance-practice movement, not intrinsic quality change, drove the revaluation — identify the enabling technology to predict the next revival.
insights.locator: Naturally, Mahler is far from unique in this.

insights.claim: Shostakovich's Leningrad Symphony waited 40 years between its second Proms performance as wartime propaganda in 1943 and its third on its own merits in 1983, showing reception can be gated by political context rather than musical merit.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: Political framing can suppress a work for decades and then release it — the same dynamic applies to any asset whose reception is entangled with geopolitics.

insights.claim: Since the millennium there have been signs that Lili Boulanger and Erich Korngold, among others, are creeping back into the Proms repertoire — the author's named candidates for the next upward re-rating.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: Two specific, named forward candidates with an observable tracking metric (Proms programming frequency) — an actionable watchlist.
insights.locator: Since the millennium, there have been signs

insights.claim: The author argues directly against the political claim that the canon is fixed by institutional 'gatekeepers', noting that within living memory many broadcasters, critics, performers and scholars were adamant Mahler should not be admitted, yet other gatekeepers made his case and the music-loving public gradually then overwhelmingly agreed.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: Reframes gatekeepers as a competitive market rather than a cartel — the canon updates through contested advocacy, so exclusion is not permanent.
insights.quote: The canon, it turns out, is not immutable, and gatekeepers admit as well as exclude.

insights.claim: The general lesson drawn is that it is rash to assume what we hear now is what we have always heard, or that the modern concert-hall canon is fixed or even very old.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: Treat any apparently permanent consensus as a recent and reversible construction — the transferable investing discipline in the piece.
insights.locator: Still, from second-rate oddball to pinnacle

insights.claim: The immensity and ubiquity of Mahler's symphonies have made Beethoven, Brahms and Schubert sound like chamber music, collapsing the perspective in which Mahler expected his own music to be heard.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: A dominant new entrant reprices the perception of everything around it — the crowding-out effect that follows any successful re-rating.
insights.quote: The immensity and ubiquity of Mahler’s symphonies have made Beethoven, Brahms and Schubert sound like chamber music.

insights.claim: Mahler's imaginative world assumes deep knowledge of Beethoven, Brahms, Schubert, Gluck, Weber and Johann Strauss, composers we now hear less because audiences have been conditioned to crave size and a certain kind of sublimity — that is, to crave Mahler.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: Demand for scale becomes self-reinforcing and erodes the very context that made the flagship work legible — a feedback loop worth spotting in any taste-driven market.
insights.locator: His imaginative world assumes a deep knowledge

insights.claim: The author mourns the era when a rare Mahler performance was a keenly awaited adventure and questions whether sounds and emotions once startling in their strangeness should ever have become quite so routine.
insights.speaker: Richard Bratby
insights.so_what: Scarcity was part of the experienced value; abundance delivers access while destroying the premium — a general trade-off in cultural distribution.
insights.locator: A happy outcome? Unquestionably, if you love the music.
